unit.title: Living things
unit.blurb: Bones, skeletons, muscles, animals with and without a backbone, and staying healthy.

O1.t: Know that some animals have a skeleton of bones, and name some bones (skull, ribs, spine).

O2.t: Describe the jobs of a skeleton: support, protection and movement.

O3.t: Know that muscles pull on bones to move them, and that muscles work in pairs.

O4.t: Sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates, and know that some animals have a skeleton outside.

O5.t: Know that germs can spread infections, how to stop them spreading, and how to use medicines safely.

captions: Hello, super scientists!
Today we are going inside your body.
This is lesson 1.1: bones and skeletons.
Let's try something.
Squeeze your hand gently. Can you feel something hard inside?
Now tap your knee. Is it hard or soft?
Touch your chin. Hard again!
Those hard parts are your bones.
You have lots of bones.
All your bones together make your skeleton.
Your skull is the bone around your brain. It is like a helmet!
Your ribs make a cage around your heart and lungs.
Pause and think.
What do all your bones together make?
Your bones are different sizes.
The longest bone is in your leg. It is called the thigh bone.
The smallest bone is inside your ear. It is as small as a grain of rice!
And guess what? A baby has more bones than you. Some of them join together as the baby grows.
Did you know?
A grown-up has two hundred and six bones. That is a lot of bones!
Joke time!
Why didn't the skeleton go to the party?
Because he had no body to go with!
Your turn.
Which bone protects your brain?
Let's go on a bone hunt!
Find a partner, and gently feel your arms and legs.
Can you feel the bones in your head and your back?
Now draw the bones you found.
Let's remember.
Bones are the hard parts inside your body.
All your bones together make your skeleton.
Your skull protects your brain.
And your ribs protect your heart and lungs.
Great work, bone detectives!

captions: Hello again, super scientists!
Why do we need a skeleton? Let's find out.
This is lesson 1.2: why we need a skeleton.
Imagine you had no bones at all.
You would be floppy, like a jellyfish!
Your skeleton holds you up, so you can stand tall.
It is like the poles inside a tent.
Your skeleton has three big jobs.
Job one: it supports your body and gives it shape.
Job two: it protects soft parts inside, like your brain and your heart.
Job three: it helps you move.
Pause and think.
What would happen to your body without a skeleton?
Feel the middle of your back.
Those bumps are your spine, or backbone.
Your spine is made of lots of small bones, like a chain.
That is why you can bend down and touch your toes!
Did you know?
A giraffe's neck is very long.
But it has the same number of neck bones as you. Just seven! Each one is very big.
Riddle time!
What has a spine, but no bones?
A book! The spine of a book is the part that holds the pages.
Your turn.
Your skull covers your brain. Which job is your skull doing?
Let's make a paper skeleton.
Ask an adult to help you cut out paper bones.
Join them together with paper pins, so the parts can move.
Where does your skeleton bend?
Let's remember.
Your skeleton supports your body and gives it shape.
It protects soft parts, like your brain and your heart.
It helps you move.
And your spine is made of many small bones. Fantastic work!

captions: Hello, strong scientists!
Bones cannot move on their own. They need helpers.
This is lesson 1.3: skeletons and muscles.
Bend your arm, like a superhero.
Put your other hand on the top of your arm.
Can you feel it getting hard and fat?
That is a muscle working!
Muscles are joined to your bones.
When a muscle pulls, the bone moves.
Bones meet at joints, like your elbow and your knee. Joints let you bend.
Pause and think.
What do muscles do to move your bones?
Muscles work in pairs, like a team.
To bend your arm, the top muscle contracts. It gets short and fat.
The muscle underneath relaxes.
To straighten your arm, they swap jobs!
Did you know?
You use lots of muscles in your face when you smile.
So smile! It is good exercise!
Joke time!
Why did the muscle go to school?
To get a little stronger at learning!
Your turn.
What do we call the place where two bones meet?
Let's give our muscles a workout!
Walk on the spot, then jump ten times.
Which muscles feel tired? Your legs?
Exercise makes muscles strong. Remember to rest and drink water.
Let's remember.
Muscles pull on bones to move them.
Bones meet at joints, so we can bend.
Muscles work in pairs. One contracts and one relaxes.
And exercise makes your muscles strong. Super strong work!

sections.title: Different kinds of skeletons

q.prompt: What do we call animals with a backbone?

stops.note: Paused on the “Pause and think” card.

captions: Hello, animal explorers!
Do all animals have bones like us? Let's find out.
This is lesson 1.4: different kinds of skeletons.
Many animals have a backbone, just like you.
A fish has a backbone. So does a frog.
A bird has a backbone too.
And so does a dog! Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates.
Some animals have no backbone. They are called invertebrates.
A worm has no bones at all. It is soft and wiggly!
A snail has a hard shell on the outside to protect it.
A crab wears its skeleton on the outside, like a suit of armour!
Pause and think.
What do we call animals with a backbone?
Insects are invertebrates too.
A ladybird has a hard outside.
So does an ant, and a grasshopper.
Their hard outside protects their soft body inside.
Did you know?
An octopus has no bones at all.
It can squeeze its body through a hole as small as a coin!
Riddle time!
What animal carries its house on its back?
A snail, of course!
Your turn.
Which animal has no backbone?
Let's sort some animals.
Look at each animal. Does it have a backbone?
Put the animals into two groups: backbone, and no backbone.
Which group is bigger?
Let's remember.
Vertebrates are animals with a backbone, like fish, birds and dogs.
Invertebrates have no backbone.
Some, like crabs and insects, have a hard skeleton on the outside.
And a worm has no skeleton at all. Wonderful work, animal experts!

captions: Hello, health heroes!
How do we stay healthy? Let's find out.
This is lesson 1.5: medicines and germs.
Sam has a cold. He sneezes. Achoo!
Tiny germs fly out into the air.
Germs are so small that we cannot see them.
The next day, his friend has a cold too. The germs spread!
We can stop germs from spreading.
Wash your hands with soap and water.
Cover your sneeze with a tissue, or your elbow.
Then put the tissue in the bin.
Pause and think.
What is the best way to get rid of germs on your hands?
When we are ill, a doctor may give us medicine.
Medicines can help us get better.
Vaccines help stop us from catching some illnesses.
Remember: only take medicine from a trusted adult. Medicines are not sweets!
Did you know?
To wash away germs, wash your hands for twenty seconds.
That is as long as singing Happy Birthday two times!
Joke time!
What did one germ say to the other germ?
Watch out, here comes the soap!
Your turn.
Who should give you medicine?
Let's pretend glitter is germs!
Put a little glitter on your hands. Then wash them with water only.
Is there still glitter? Now wash with soap and water.
Which way got rid of the most glitter?
Let's remember.
Germs are tiny living things that can make us ill.
Germs can spread from one person to another.
Washing your hands with soap stops germs.
And only take medicine from a trusted adult. Brilliant work, health heroes!
